title: Dynamic memory: new and delete

visuals.title: Match the word to its meaning

pairs.meaning: Make an int box on the heap holding 5 and return its address
Give the heap box back to the computer
A pointer value that means: points to nothing
Heap memory you no longer have an address for and never deleted
A pointer that still holds the address of memory that was already deleted
Deleting the same box twice: a serious error (undefined behaviour)

goal: After this you can create a variable on the heap with new, use it through a pointer, give it back with delete, and avoid memory leaks and dangling pointers.
warmup: Think of a rented hall for a wedding. You book it when you need it (new), you get a key with the address written on it (the pointer), and when the function is over you must return the hall (delete). If you lose the key without returning the hall, nobody can use it and you keep paying: that is a memory leak. If you return the hall but keep walking to the old address, you find strangers there: that is a dangling pointer.
definition: Dynamic memory allocation means asking for memory WHILE the program is running. You need it when the size is known only at run time (for example the user types how many students), or when data must stay alive after the function that created it has ended. The operator new takes a box from the heap and returns its address, so you keep the answer in a pointer. The operator delete gives the box back. Local variables live on the stack and disappear automatically. Heap boxes live until you delete them.
howItWorks: Step 1: new int(5) finds a free int-sized place on the heap, puts 5 in it, and returns its address. Step 2: you store that address in a pointer, for example int *p = new int(5);. The pointer p is a normal variable on the stack. The box it points to is on the heap. Step 3: you use the box with *p, exactly like an ordinary variable. Step 4: when you are done, delete p; gives the box back. After delete, the pointer p still holds the old address, but the box is no longer yours, so p is a dangling pointer. Good habit: write p = nullptr; straight after delete. Rules to remember: every new needs exactly one delete, never use a pointer after delete, never delete the same address twice (double delete), and never overwrite the only pointer to a box with another address, or the old box is lost (leak). Initialisation: new int; gives an unknown value, new int(5); gives 5, new int(); gives 0.

worked.problem: Create an int on the heap with value 5, print it, add 10, print it again, then delete it and set the pointer to nullptr. Show that the pointer now equals nullptr.
pseudocode: IF p is nullptr THEN PRINT message
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B["p = new int(5)"]
  B --> C[/"Print *p"/]
  C --> D["*p = *p + 10"]
  D --> E[/"Print *p"/]
  E --> F["delete p"]
  F --> G["p = nullptr"]
  G --> H{"p == nullptr?"}
  H -->|Yes| I[/"Print p points to nothing"/]
  I --> J([End])

sample.title: One int on the heap: new, use, delete
sample.expectedOutput:
Value: 5
Now: 15
p points to nothing

explanation.text: new int(5) makes an int box on the heap holding 5 and returns its address. p is an ordinary pointer stored on the stack.
*p follows the address in p to the heap box, so it prints 5.
The heap box is used just like a normal variable, only through *p.
delete gives the heap box back. It does not erase p itself.
After delete, point p to nullptr so it cannot be used by mistake.
We can safely test a pointer for nullptr. We must never dereference it.

steps.note: The program starts. Nothing is on the heap yet.
new asks the heap for one int box, puts 5 inside, and gives back its address. p stores that address.
*p means: go to the address in p and read the box. It holds 5.
Read 5 from the heap box, add 10, write 15 back into the same box.
The heap box now holds 15.
The heap box is given back. p still holds the old address, so p is now a dangling pointer. Never use *p after this.
We set p to nullptr so it clearly points to nothing.
p == nullptr is true, so the if body runs.
Safe check passed.
Program ends. Every new had a delete, so no leak.

explanation.text: No value given: the box holds garbage until we assign. That is why the next line writes 7.
Assign after allocating.
Allocate and initialise in one step with round brackets.
Empty round brackets give the value 0 for numbers.

worked.problem: Write a function makeBox that creates an int on the heap with a given start value and returns it. In main make two boxes (10 and 20), store their sum in the first, print both, and free everything correctly.
pseudocode: set x and y to nullptr
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B["x = makeBox(10)"]
  B --> C["y = makeBox(20)"]
  C --> D["*x = *x + *y"]
  D --> E[/"Print *x and *y"/]
  E --> F["delete x and y"]
  F --> G["x = y = nullptr"]
  G --> H([End])

sample.title: Heap data outlives the function that made it

explanation.text: The function returns an int pointer: the address of a heap box.
The box is created on the heap, so it does not die when makeBox ends. A normal local variable would.
We return the address, not the box. The caller now owns the box and must delete it.
x receives the address of the first box.
Two separate boxes, read through two pointers.
The caller is responsible for the delete, because makeBox gave the box away.
Clean up the pointers after delete.

steps.note: main calls makeBox(10). A new stack frame appears with start = 10.
new makes a heap box holding 10. box (on the stack) stores its address.
The function returns the ADDRESS. The frame of makeBox vanishes, but heap box A stays alive. x now owns it.
The same again: a second heap box B holding 20 is created and y points to it.
10 + 20 = 30 is stored in box A. Box B is unchanged.
Prints the two heap values.
Box A is returned to the heap.
Box B is returned too.
Both pointers are set to nullptr. No leaks, no dangling pointers.

variations.when: You will assign the value yourself right after. Until then the box holds garbage.
You want the box to start with a known value.
Curly-bracket initialisation, same meaning as round brackets.
Always, when you are finished with the box.

variations.way: Return a heap pointer from a function
variations.when: The data must outlive the function. The caller must delete it.

mistakes.error: No compiler message. The program runs, but the 4 bytes are never returned: a memory leak. In a long program that runs for hours many leaks fill the memory.
Usually no compiler message. After delete the box is not yours. Reading it is undefined behaviour: it may print garbage or crash.
No compiler message, but deleting the same address twice is undefined behaviour and often crashes the program at run time. (This is why we set p = nullptr after delete.)
error: invalid conversion from 'int*' to 'int' [-fpermissive]. new returns an address, so the variable on the left must be a pointer.
No compiler message. The first box (5) has no pointer any more, so it can never be deleted: a leak. Delete before you reuse the pointer.

examTips: Say the pair out loud: every new must have a matching delete. Examiners look for it.
After delete write p = nullptr; and mention that it avoids a dangling pointer.
new returns an address, so the left side is always a pointer: int *p = new int(5);
Stack variables are freed automatically at the end of the function. Heap variables are freed only by delete.
Know the three problems by name: memory leak (forgot delete), dangling pointer (used after delete), double delete (deleted twice).
romanSummary: Dynamic memory ka matlab hai program chalte waqt heap se memory maangna, jab size pehle se maloom na ho ya data function ke baad bhi zinda rakhna ho.
new heap par box banata hai aur uska address wapas deta hai, jise hum pointer mein rakhte hain: int *p = new int(5);
Kaam khatam hone par delete p; likhte hain aur phir p = nullptr; taake dangling pointer na bane.
delete bhool gaye to memory leak hota hai. Ek address ko do dafa delete karna (double delete) bhi ghalat hai.
Har new ke saath ek delete zaroor likhein.

practice.prompt: Which operator takes memory from the heap while the program is running?
practice.explanation: new allocates heap memory and returns its address. delete gives it back.

options: The address of the new int box
practice.answer: The address of the new int box
practice.hint: That is why the left side is a pointer.
practice.explanation: new always returns the address of the memory it created. The value 5 lives inside the box.

practice.hint: p and q hold the same address.
practice.explanation: q is a second pointer to the SAME box. Writing 9 through q changes the box that p also sees.

practice.answer: The first box (5) is lost because p was overwritten without delete: a memory leak. Fix: delete p; before p = new int(6);
practice.hint: Count the new and the delete.
practice.explanation: Two new, one delete. The box holding 5 can no longer be reached, so it can never be deleted.
delete p; returns the heap box. Then p = nullptr; makes p safe.

practice.prompt: Write code that allocates a double on the heap with value 2.5, prints its value multiplied by 2, then frees it.
practice.explanation: new double(2.5) makes the box, *d reads it (2.5 * 2 = 5), delete d frees it.

practice.hint: After b = a, both pointers hold the same address.
practice.explanation: *a becomes 6. Then b is given a's address, so both print 6. (The old box of b was lost: a leak.)

practice.prompt: Why do we need dynamic memory?
options: The size may be known only at run time, or the data must outlive a function
It makes the program run faster than the stack always
Because the stack has no variables
Because pointers cannot point to local variables
practice.answer: The size may be known only at run time, or the data must outlive a function
practice.explanation: Stack sizes are fixed at compile time. The heap lets us decide while running and keep data after a function returns.

quiz.prompt: What does a memory leak mean?
options: Heap memory that was never deleted and can no longer be reached
A pointer that points to nullptr
Using a variable before declaring it
quiz.answer: Heap memory that was never deleted and can no longer be reached
quiz.explanation: Forgetting delete leaves the box allocated with no way to return it.

quiz.prompt: After delete p; what is the best next line?
quiz.explanation: p still holds the old address. Setting it to nullptr avoids a dangling pointer.

options: A pointer that holds the address of memory that was already deleted
A pointer to a global variable
quiz.answer: A pointer that holds the address of memory that was already deleted
quiz.hint: The box is gone but the address remains.

quiz.explanation: The variable that receives an address must be a pointer.

quiz.prompt: What happens when you run delete p; twice on the same address?
quiz.hint: The box is already gone after the first delete.
quiz.explanation: Double delete is a serious error. Setting p = nullptr after the first delete makes the second one harmless.
